title: How do you work with compound growth and CAGR without a calculator?
description: Compound growth explained for case interviews: CAGR, quick multipliers, the rule of 72, and a table of growth factors you can memorise.
hook: Growth over several years compounds, and simple approximations are usually good enough in an interview, as long as you know which ones to use. Here is a toolkit for compound growth without a calculator.
body:
The idea

Growing 10% a year for two years is not 20% in total; it is 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, or 21%. Each year grows on top of the last.

Growth factors worth memorising

Yearly growthAfter 3 yearsAfter 5 years
5%×1.16×1.28
10%×1.33×1.61
15%×1.52×2.01
20%×1.73×2.49

Working out CAGR

Revenue grew from £100M to £161M in five years. From the table, ×1.61 over five years is about 10% a year. Without a table, guess a round rate, test it, and adjust (see the growth trick).

The rule of 72

Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate. At 8%, about 9 years. At 12%, about 6. It also works backwards: to double in 4 years, you need about 18% a year.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing total growth by the number of years.
  • Forgetting that a 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover.
